As of 245 PM EDT Friday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Rain chances increase Saturday night into Sunday as 
the remnants of Hurricane Isaias move farther inland.

Hurricane Isaias has been upgraded to a major (Category 3) hurricane 
across the northern Gulf. Isaias is expected to make landfall along 
the far western FL Panhandle near the FL/GA border tonight before 
weakening as it lifts north through AL Sat. Isaias is expected to 
weaken to a Tropical Depression Sat night into Sunday as it moves NE 
across TN towards the KY/OH/WV border. As the extratropical 
transition occurs, the precip shield will expand in coverage across 
the local area, likely providing a beneficial rain for most areas. 
Ahead of the rain, clouds ahead of Isaias have already moved over 
the local area, with mostly cloudy skies expected to continue 
through Sun. However, rain will likely hold off until late Sat or 
Sat night given high pressure over the area. High pressure centered 
over the area today will gradually lift NE through Sun. As it does 
so, a CAD setup will develop with a warm front initially across the 
Carolinas Sun morning which will gradually lift north through the 
day. Ahead of the front, the airmass will likely be too stable to 
support thunderstorms or severe weather. Instead, widespread light 
to moderate rain will spread north late Sat afternoon into Sat night 
with PoPs increasing to 70-100% late Sat night into Sun morning. 
However, most of the day Sat will likely be dry.

Stratiform rain early Sun morning gradually becomes more showery by 
late morning as the warm front begins to lift into southern portions 
of the area. While it's still early for high confidence in 
specifics, models show the potential for a lull in the precip Sun 
afternoon behind the warm front with a second round of showers and 
perhaps storms developing along a pseudo cold front late Sun 
afternoon into Sun evening. As such, Sun may not be a complete 
washout. Additionally, if there is lull in precip Sun afternoon and 
destabilization is able to occur, a conditional severe risk could 
develop late in the day. The 12km NAM and RRFS show the potential 
for a broken band of supercells developing across the southern 
Piedmont late Sun afternoon, spreading east into early Sun night. If 
supercells do develop, the main risk would be for a brief tornado. 
However, strong winds are also possible. For now, the greatest 
severe potential appears to be with this late round of convection, 
however, a low-end tornado threat also exists along the warm front 
as it lifts north across the area given the increased SRH along the 
front. To account for this potential, SPC has a Marginal (level 1/5) 
risk for severe weather across the entire FA. However, this may need 
to be refined as we get closer. For instance, the northern Piedmont 
may hold on to the CAD longer than models show, which would limit 
any destabilization potential there. Otherwise, the main 
limiting factors for the late day severe risk are that surface 
winds are expected to be less backed (S/SSE versus SE/E) behind 
the front, destabilization may be hindered by widespread rain, 
and the timing is favored to be late in the day (likely after 
sunset for most of the area). Nevertheless, tropical remnants 
have a well-documented history of producing tornadoes, so the 
threat will need to be closely monitored.

Outside of the severe risk, heavy rain and localized flooding is 
possible given the tropical moisture. The current forecast has 
rainfall totals of 1-2" for most of the area. However, the greatest 
potential for flash flooding is across far SE VA/NE NC where a 
longer duration in the warm sector is possible. Here, a corridor 
of 2-3" with localized totals of 3-4"+ are possible. Farther 
inland, the lingering CAD through most of the event should keep 
rain rates more limited. Additionally, quite a bit of model 
guidance (including the EPS) shows a swath of localized minimum 
rainfall totals across portions of central VA with rainfall 
totals closer to 1" for the event. As such, while there is a 
Marginal ERO (excessive rainfall outlook) across far SE VA/NE NC
Sat (for the Sat night rain) and a marginal ERO all the way to 
the I-95 corridor Sun, confidence is highest across SE VA/NE NC
(including the Hampton Roads region). Showers taper off from W 
to E Sun night with dry conditions returning by Mon.

Otherwise, E winds of 5-10 mph inland and 10-15 mph with gusts up to 
20-25 mph along the coast Sat increase to 10-15 mph with gusts up to 
20-25 mph inland and 15-20 mph with gusts up to 30-35 mph along the 
coast late Sat night into early Sun. The strongest winds look to be 
along and just north of the warm front as it lifts north across the 
area. Winds become SSE/SE and remain breezy (especially along the 
coast) Sun afternoon. Highs this afternoon are expected to be in the
